# Round3: blocking CUDA events and pinned readback rejected

The named remaining lead was measured and **did not reduce host CPU in this installed WSL/PyTorch/CUDA environment**. Default and blocking CUDA events both consumed nearly their full wait duration as thread CPU. A bounded pinned destination + nonblocking D2H copy + blocking completion event also showed no CPU benefit. Do not integrate the event candidate or implement the more complex per-job pinned-readback path on this evidence. The independently accepted round2 implementation remains experimental opt-in with defaults unchanged.

No model/server was launched. The user-authorized five-model follow-through was conditional on a meaningful tiny-gate reduction, which did not occur. Existing round2 product results and their limitations remain attached to round2 source; there is no round3 ARC/throughput improvement measurement. The substantial continuous executor CPU finding remains an observed limitation. This negative gate closes this particular proposed remedy, not proof that every possible optimization is exhausted. Root owns the new independent Astra review and integration decision.

## Comparison and result

Three fixed pairs per method, order default/blocking, blocking/default, default/blocking; no outcome-based selection. Same producer stream, identical tensor values and queued dependencies. Default readback executes `tolist()` on the actual producer/scoring stream. Blocking readback queues `pinned.copy_(data, non_blocking=True)` on that stream, records `torch.cuda.Event(blocking=True)`, synchronizes it, then reads the pinned CPU tensor. The fixed result is 2×11 float32, 88 pinned bytes, representing the retained small-pool output shape. It is a wait-mechanism diagnostic, not an inference or semantic-ranking test.

A first valid main-thread check used 8,000,000 CUDA delay cycles (~2.6ms observed wait). A second fixed confirmation used 32,000,000 cycles (~10.4ms), waiting in a ThreadPoolExecutor thread, to check executor behavior and a longer outstanding dependency. Both modes use the same delay within each comparison. Every valid case asserts the event is outstanding immediately after enqueue, and every readback returns exact expected values. The executor test creates its worker after this pending check; wait timing excludes thread construction. Readiness-only cases do not copy or read scores. The 24 measured waits total 0.157s of host wait envelopes; this is not measured GPU busy time. Two valid CUDA processes plus one failed fixture process were launched, each bounded by 45s including context startup. Actual total context/lifecycle wall time was not separately recorded. No warmup loops, serving lifecycles, settings changes or profiler/kernel sweeps were run.

Values are mean **wall ms / thread CPU ms**, three samples each. The small differences are descriptive; no significance or universal driver-behavior claim follows.

| Fixture | Phase | Default | Blocking / pinned | CPU change |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Main thread, ~2.6ms | readiness | 2.618 / 2.618 | 2.639 / 2.639 | +0.79% |
| Main thread, ~2.6ms | readback | 2.661 / 2.606 | 2.629 / 2.629 | +0.90% |
| Executor, ~10.4ms | readiness | 10.357 / 10.354 | 10.414 / 10.411 | +0.55% |
| Executor, ~10.4ms | readback | 10.460 / 10.016 | 10.424 / 10.424 | +4.07% |

The blocking flag did not produce the hoped-for CPU drop at either dependency length. In the executor readback control, the first default readback has slightly lower thread CPU; nothing here favors the pinned alternative. No latency/age/drop tradeoff was measured in a model because the prerequisite CPU reduction failed.

The installed build is PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 / CUDA13.0. `torch.cuda.Event.__new__` forwards `blocking`, its synchronize calls the C++ base, and the installed c10 header uses `cudaEventSynchronize`. This experiment uses `torch.cuda.Event`, not generic `torch.Event`. The Python binding implementation source and direct runtime flag introspection were unavailable in the inspected files. We therefore report observed behavior under the requested public API, not a proven driver cause or a claim that the flag was ignored. No CUDA scheduling/global configuration was changed.

## Correctness, failures and source status

- Final native CPU suite: **366 passed**, with CUDA initialization explicitly forbidden. This comprises the prior363 plus three round3 regressions for host-readiness construction, endpoints before observer bookkeeping, and additive Kineto/aggregate scope nesting. CPU tests cover the existing scoring methods, conservative workspace budgets, transported generations/residencies/expiry and actual constrained scheduler/manager path; they do not qualify a new GPU readback pipeline.
- Initial CPU collection failed because the copied driver lacked `hooks/funnel.py` and a new test named the profiler class incorrectly. Task-local setup was repaired; original failure receipt retained.
- Initial CUDA fixture failed an exact-value assertion because its control called `tolist()` on the default stream while the producer was on a nondefault stream. This was a fixture dependency bug, not a production scoring result. The corrected control uses the producer stream. The invalid version and native failure receipt are retained. The longer executor confirmation changes only the declared delay/thread context; it does not retune a serving workload.
- Round3 candidate changes only the owned query/snapshot readiness event flags plus optional observer endpoint accounting; source/summary fences and scoring math, ties, nonfinite handling, cadence, expiry, identities, capacity and admission are unchanged. The readiness changes are **rejected**. No per-job pinned readback implementation, memory-budget change, buffer pool or new cancellation/failure lifetime was introduced. Thus the proposed stronger adversarial partial-enqueue ownership fixture did not advance: no changed ownership/readback path passed the benefit gate. Round2's accepted source and its previously disclosed stress-fixture limits remain unchanged; we make no new allocation-reuse, poison, failure or all-method GPU-score safety claim.
- Optional observer-only patches are separately exportable. Host CPU endpoint is taken before host wall endpoint, before event bookkeeping and aggregation; aggregate scopes wrap tracing instead of being replaced. The additive nesting regression passes. No model diagnostic exercised this observer change, so it is not a measured final full-component correction. Product profiling stays off and defaults are unchanged.

## Relation to round2 and deferred work

Round2's continuous diagnostic remains 1030 published jobs/11 full-queue drops; 1013 aggregate jobs recorded readiness11.373s wall/11.332s CPU and readback5.822s wall/5.806s CPU. Inclusive executor/readback scopes overlap and must not be added. Round3 did not remeasure those component totals or close the missing17 aggregate-job measurement retrospectively. Existing round2 products passed their small paired screen (+0.311%/+0.396% throughput) with zero organic competitive async jobs; those products cannot establish reduced continuous scoring CPU or ranking benefit. No new correctness/output/native-key/transfer checks from serving are claimed. The round2 evidence preserves those checks for its exact source.

No further GPU work is proposed in this task. The remaining large-pool, summary-schema, index and capacity leads are deferred as root/Astra directed. Preserved negative evidence is sufficient to reject this named low-complexity remedy in the tested environment without adding a new asynchronous subsystem or pretending off-path CPU disappeared.

## Evidence and reproducibility

- `evidence/tiny-comparison-short.json`, `evidence/tiny-comparison.json`, `tiny-measurements.csv`, `evidence/gate-analysis.json`: all sample values and paired deltas.
- `tiny_compare.py`: exact measured executor script. `tiny_compare_short.py` and `tiny_compare_invalid_stream.py` reconstruct the earlier successful/failed fixture variants from the measured executor source and retained command history; they were not contemporaneously hash-frozen. The final candidate pins are also after the tiny gate; no pre-run hash-freeze claim is made for these tiny source variants.
- `evidence/cpu-final-with-hook-test.activity.json`, `evidence/cpu-validation.json`: actual-runtime366-pass CUDA-forbidden validation; prior failure receipts remain.
- `accepted-round2-full.patch` and `evidence/accepted-source-pins.json`: unchanged accepted source. `rejected-full.patch` and `rejected-round2-delta.patch`: rejected experiment plus observer/test changes, clearly unsuitable for automatic integration. Both reconstruct all candidate Python files exactly under native git-apply check/application. `optional-profiler-endpoints.patch`, `optional-additive-trace.patch`: separately reviewable observer fixes.
- `evidence/candidate-pins.json` pins rejected round3 source. The inherited `candidate/candidate-pins.json` is historical and nonauthoritative. `evidence/installed-event-source.json` pins inspected installed event sources; environment/runtime pins are retained without copying binaries/models.
- `handback.tar.gz` is losslessly compressed and every member hash verified. `MANIFEST.json`/`handback-sha256.json` identify it. Final native release, queue cleanup and postarchive verification receipts are in a separate `cleanup-receipts.tar.gz` to keep the main archive immutable.

Fresh native CPU-light, quiet and analysis-light sessions were used serially. Project lock was acquired after admission by each CPU/CUDA fixture. Each activity was mediated, finite and renewed at milestones; quiet restoration/release completed immediately after the failed-benefit gate, before reporting. No expired/uncertain grant was resumed. Final cleanup receipts establish empty owned descendants, free project lock, exact protected-source restoration, native release and obsolete own-wait cleanup. Shared notification worker, caches/model/runtime/settings/other owners and all earlier evidence are preserved. Storage steward inventories only round3 and removes owned bytecode; separate native Windows and WSL free-byte measurements are in `evidence/storage-handback.json`. Changes in free space are observed filesystem deltas, not proof of physical VHDX reclamation.
